explanation: A bootleg app is a paid app with its DRM removed, and bootleggers often add malware to make money. Sideloading an APK also skips the vetting of the official store. The app should be removed and the phone scanned.
whyWrong: Battery drain may be a symptom, but the main concern is malware and data theft.
An app does not need to change the orientation lock, and that is not a security concern.
Jailbreaking applies to iOS; Android can install an APK when unknown sources are allowed.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter) – Core 2 Chapter 7: Troubleshooting Operating Systems and Security; CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 55: Troubleshooting Mobile Operating Systems Security Issues

stem: The MDM console flags a company Android phone. The technician finds that USB debugging is on and a mock location app is selected, so the phone reports that it is inside the office geofence when it is not. What should the technician do to BEST resolve the issue?
options: Turn off Developer options and USB debugging on the phone
Clear the cache of the mapping app
Turn on Airplane mode while the user is out of the office
explanation: Developer mode allows USB debugging and mock GPS locations, which can be used to get around location-based security. Turning off Developer options removes those settings. The phone can then report its real status to the MDM.
whyWrong: Clearing a mapping app's cache does not remove the mock location setting.
Airplane mode cuts off the phone's connections but leaves the developer settings in place.
The screen timeout saves power and has nothing to do with the location setting.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter) – Core 2 Chapter 7: Troubleshooting Operating Systems and Security

stem: Which of the following are possible symptoms of malware? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Malware can have many symptoms. Viruses are especially prevalent in today’s society; there are millions of different kinds. Fake security alerts, failure to update Windows, and renamed system files are all possible symptoms of malware—specifically, viruses.
whyWrong: A preinstallation environment is a tool for deploying and repairing Windows, not a symptom.
A rogue antivirus is itself malware, not a symptom of it.
User error can cause an infection, but it is not a symptom of malware.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – A+ Core 2 (220-1202) Practice Exam, Practice Exam question 40

stem: You have been tasked with running updates on a Windows computer. Some of the updates go through fine, but one of them fails. While troubleshooting, you restart the computer and attempt to install the failed update, but it continues to fail. Which of the following should you do FIRST?
options: Analyze the Event Viewer for more information about the failures.
Download the failed update to install it manually.
Visit the Microsoft Update website to see if there is an issue with a specific update.
Look up the error number associated with the failed update.
explanation: The first thing you should do is look up the error number. If an item fails during Windows Update, an error log called WindowsUpdate.log can be written to C:\Windows\Logs\WindowsUpdate, but only if you have run the Get-WindowsUpdateLog cmdlet in PowerShell first. An example of an error code is 0x80243FFF, which is a user interface error. You might also need to access the CBS.log file, which is located in %systemroot%\Logs.
whyWrong: The Event Viewer is too general; the update error code points to the exact cause.
Installing the same update manually will probably give the same error.
There is no Microsoft Update website for this; the error code is looked up on Microsoft's support pages.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – A+ Core 2 (220-1202) Practice Exam, Practice Exam question 59
note: OS update failures are listed under 220-1202 3.4 (common symptoms); the classification gave 3.1.

stem: A user reports encountering sporadic, seemingly non-malicious advertisement notifications within the Windows 10 Action Center. These notifications suggest that the advertisements originate from a web browser. What is the MOST effective solution for a technician to implement?
options: Deactivate the browser’s ability to send notifications to the Action Center
Perform a comprehensive antivirus scan on the computer
Turn off all notifications within the Action Center
Transfer specific site notifications from the Allowed category to Block
explanation: The most effective solution for the technician to implement in this scenario is to disable the browser’s capability to send notifications to the Windows 10 Action Center. By doing so, the unwanted advertisement notifications originating from the browser will no longer appear within the Action Center, providing relief to the user. This solution directly targets the source of the notifications, ensuring a focused resolution.
whyWrong: The notifications are not malicious, so an antivirus scan does not target the cause.
Turning off all notifications is too broad and hides useful messages.
Blocking sites one by one does not stop the browser from sending more ads.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 11: Mock Exam: Core 2 (220-1102), Mock Exam question 3
note: 220-1102 3.2; mapped to 220-1202 3.4 (PC security troubleshooting).

stem: A user is experiencing frequent popups on their web browser. What will offer the BEST solution to remediate this problem? (Choose two.)
options: Install a reputable ad blocker extension
Update the browser to the latest version
Ignore the popups; they are harmless
Download and run a registry cleaner tool
Reset the computer to factory settings
explanation: Installing a reputable ad blocker extension can effectively block unwanted pop-up ads and enhance the user’s browsing experience by preventing intrusive ads from appearing. Outdated browsers may have vulnerabilities that allow popups and other unwanted content to appear. Updating the browser to the latest version often includes security fixes that can help prevent such issues.
whyWrong: Disabling the firewall leaves the computer open to threats and does not stop pop-ups.
Pop-ups can be a sign of malware, so they should not be ignored.
Registry cleaners can do harm and do not fix the cause of pop-ups.
A factory reset is a last resort that erases data and settings.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 11: Mock Exam: Core 2 (220-1102), Mock Exam question 17
note: 220-1102 3.2; mapped to 220-1202 3.4 (PC security troubleshooting).

stem: Which tool will allow you to diagnose why Windows Update keeps failing?
explanation: Windows Update Troubleshooter can assist in diagnosing problems with Windows Update. The ntbtlog.txt file is used to diagnose problems with bootup. Windows Recovery Environment is used to solve problems with Windows and is not typically used for problems with Windows Updates. Safe mode is a boot mode that loads minimal drivers and services.
whyWrong: The ntbtlog.txt file logs the drivers loaded at boot; it does not diagnose Windows Update.
The Windows Recovery Environment repairs Windows startup problems and is not the usual tool for update failures.
Safe mode loads minimal drivers and services; it does not diagnose why updates fail.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter), Volume 2 – Chapter 7: Troubleshooting Operating Systems and Security, Review Questions question 12

stem: Which of the following tools allows you to manually fix maliciously modified system files?
explanation: The System File Checker (SFC) allows you to manually scan for modified operating system files and repair them. regedit is used to modify the Registry. bootrec is used to repair the boot records on an operating system installation. User Account Control (UAC) is used to control access to administrative credentials.
whyWrong: Regedit edits the Registry; it does not scan for and repair system files.
The bootrec tool repairs boot records, not modified operating system files.
UAC controls the use of administrative credentials; it does not repair system files.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter), Volume 2 – Chapter 7: Troubleshooting Operating Systems and Security, Review Questions question 14

stem: Which of the following can you do to help eliminate security problems? (Choose the BEST answer.)
options: Prevent booting into Windows Recovery Environment.
explanation: Establishing security policies and procedures will help eliminate security problems and guide employees on what to do if they arise. Optimizing drives will defragment drives and has no effect on security. Preventing booting into safe mode will only hinder diagnostics. Preventing booting into Windows Recovery Environment will also hinder diagnostics.
whyWrong: Optimizing drives defragments them and has no effect on security.
Preventing Safe Mode only makes it harder to diagnose problems.
Preventing the Windows Recovery Environment only makes it harder to repair problems.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter), Volume 2 – Chapter 7: Troubleshooting Operating Systems and Security, Review Questions question 15
note: The chapter gives this in its introduction to PC security issues; mapped to 220-1202 3.4.1.

stem: A technician coworker is using certmgr.msc to analyze a problem with a computer. Which of the following issues is the technician MOST LIKELY troubleshooting?
explanation: The technician is most likely investigating a certificate issue, which is why the tech is using the Certificate Manager (certmgr.msc). The Trusted Root CA (Certificate Authority) section in the Certificate Manager contains all the certificates that were issued to the computer by third-party companies, as well as certificates that were created on the computer itself. When double-clicked, each certificate will display the issuer and the validation dates. Make sure certificates are still valid! Delete any that are not valid and notify the appropriate companies or personnel.
whyWrong: A hijacked email account is not checked with the Certificate Manager.
Spyware is found with antimalware tools, not by reviewing certificates in certmgr.msc.
Browser redirection is caused by malware or extensions and is not examined with certmgr.msc.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 56: Troubleshooting PC Security Issues, Cram Quiz question 1

stem: Why might a user be unable to access a network from a Windows computer?
options: The computer’s Wi-Fi access point is out of range.
The network cable is securely connected.
The computer is infected with malware.
The user does not have the correct access point configured.
explanation: The computer’s Wi-Fi access point is out of range, and the user does not have the correct access point configured. The access point needs to be in range, and the device must have the correct credentials to access the network. Malware can sometimes interfere as well.
whyWrong: A securely connected network cable is what you want, so it is not a reason for losing network access.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 56: Troubleshooting PC Security Issues, Cram Quiz question 2
note: Network access problems are not a named 220-1202 3.4 symptom; mapped to the PC security symptoms, since malware is one of the causes.

stem: Why might a Windows update fail to install?
options: The computer's firewall is turned off.
The update was installed successfully but needs a restart.
There is insufficient free space on the hard drive.
The computer is connected to a VPN.
explanation: You need enough space available on your system drive to install the update successfully; otherwise, it will fail. Free up more space and try your update again.
whyWrong: A firewall that is turned off is a security risk, but it does not stop Windows updates from installing.
An update that installed and waits for a restart has not failed to install.
A VPN connection does not normally stop a Windows update from installing.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 56: Troubleshooting PC Security Issues, Cram Quiz question 3
note: OS update failures are a 220-1202 3.4 common symptom.

stem: Why might a user be experiencing excessive browser pop-ups?
options: The browser’s pop-up blocker is turned off.
The browser is in Incognito mode.
The website is listed in the browser’s trusted sites.
The computer is infected with malware or adware.
explanation: The browser is likely infected with malware. In that case, use the instructions in Chapter 46 to help clean the system. However, the browser’s pop-up blocker might have been turned off. Sometimes this is by accident, sometimes on purpose. Watch for this possibility.
whyWrong: Incognito mode only stops session data being stored locally; it does not cause pop-ups.
Adding a site to trusted sites does not by itself flood the browser with pop-ups.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 56: Troubleshooting PC Security Issues, Cram Quiz question 4

stem: Which of these is a common cause of unexpected redirection to malicious websites?
options: The browser is configured to allow third-party cookies.
The user has bookmarked the website incorrectly.
The computer is infected with malware or a malicious browser extension.
explanation: Malicious browser extensions, either as part of other malware or by themselves, often will redirect your browsing to unexpected websites. Sometimes these sites appear innocuous: a change to your search engine, for instance. Sometimes they are pages full of ads. Still other times the pages are malicious and attempt to steal data. They are always problematic.
whyWrong: Third-party cookies allow tracking, but they do not redirect the browser to malicious websites.
A wrong bookmark goes to the wrong page every time, but it is not a common cause of unexpected redirection.
Disabling JavaScript reduces what pages can do; it does not cause redirection to malicious sites.
source: CompTIA A+ Core 1 and Core 2 Exam Cram, 2nd ed. – Chapter 56: Troubleshooting PC Security Issues, Cram Quiz question 5

stem: A user’s computer is repeatedly prompted to install the latest operating system update but encounters errors during the installation process. Which of the following steps can be taken to address the OS update failures?
options: Clear temporary files and retry the update
explanation: OS update failures can sometimes occur due to conflicts with temporary files or corrupted update data. Clearing temporary files helps eliminate potential issues and provides a clean environment for the update process. After clearing the temporary files, the user can retry the update to see whether the errors are resolved.
whyWrong: A different web browser has no part in installing operating system updates.
A new power supply does not fix update errors that come from bad or leftover update files.
Screen resolution has no effect on the operating system update process.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 9: Software Troubleshooting, Objective 3.1 question 16
note: 220-1102 3.1; mapped to 220-1202 3.4 (Windows OS issues in the old objectives). OS update failures are a 220-1202 3.4 symptom.

stem: A user is unable to access the network from their personal computer (PC). Which of the following steps should a service desk technician take to troubleshoot this issue?
options: Check the physical network connections and cables
explanation: The first step in troubleshooting network connectivity issues is to verify the physical network connections and cables. This includes checking whether the network cable is securely plugged into the PC and the router or switch. By ensuring the physical connections are intact, any issues related to loose or faulty connections can be identified and resolved.
whyWrong: Updating the antivirus software does not fix a loose or failed network cable.
Reinstalling the OS is a last resort and not where network troubleshooting starts.
More RAM does not restore a lost network connection.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 9: Software Troubleshooting, Objective 3.2 question 1
note: 220-1102 3.2; mapped to 220-1202 3.4 (PC security issues in the old objectives).

stem: A user frequently receives desktop alerts warning about potential security threats, but these alerts are false positives. Which of the following steps should the technician take to address this issue?
options: Adjust the settings of the firewall
Run a full system scan using an anti-virus program
Exclude the false positive files from anti-virus scans
explanation: False alerts regarding anti-virus protection can be caused by legitimate files being flagged as threats. By excluding the false positive files from anti-virus scans, the alerts will no longer appear, and the user can distinguish between genuine threats and false positives.
whyWrong: An update may improve detection but does not stop alerts on files already known to be safe.
The firewall filters network traffic and does not produce antivirus threat alerts.
A full scan would flag the same safe files again and would not stop the false alerts.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 9: Software Troubleshooting, Objective 3.2 question 2
note: 220-1102 3.2; mapped to 220-1202 3.4 (PC security issues in the old objectives).

stem: A user reports that their personal files have been altered or are missing/renamed on their PC. Which of the following security issues is MOST LIKELY responsible for this?
options: Unauthorized access by a network intruder
explanation: A ransomware infection is a type of malware that encrypts or alters the user’s files and demands a ransom to restore access. This aligns with the user’s report of altered or missing/renamed files.
whyWrong: Phishing tricks users into giving away information and does not usually alter or rename files.
A rootkit hides itself and other malware; it does not usually rename or encrypt personal files.
An intruder could tamper with files, but ransomware is the far more common cause of altered and renamed files.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 9: Software Troubleshooting, Objective 3.2 question 3
note: 220-1102 3.2; mapped to 220-1202 3.4 (PC security issues in the old objectives).

stem: A user raises a service ticket as they are experiencing unwanted notifications within the operating system (OS) of their PC. Which of the following steps should a technician take to troubleshoot this issue?
options: Clean the registry using a registry cleaner tool
explanation: Unwanted notifications within the OS can often be caused by unnecessary or malicious programs running at startup. By disabling startup programs, the technician can eliminate programs that may be responsible for generating unwanted notifications.
whyWrong: The BIOS runs before Windows loads and has nothing to do with notifications inside the OS.
Reinstalling the OS is a drastic step to try only after simpler fixes fail.
Registry cleaners are not needed and do not remove the programs that create the notifications.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 9: Software Troubleshooting, Objective 3.2 question 4
note: 220-1102 3.2; mapped to 220-1202 3.4 (PC security issues in the old objectives).

stem: A user is encountering failures when attempting to install updates for their operating system (OS) on their PC. Which of the following steps should the technician take to resolve this issue?
options: Restart the PC and try installing the updates again
Clear the browser cache and try again
explanation: Often, issues with OS update failures can be resolved by restarting the PC and attempting to install the updates again. This can help reset any temporary glitches or conflicts that may be preventing successful updates.
whyWrong: Turning off antivirus can sometimes help, but it lowers protection and is not the first thing to try.
Reinstalling the OS from scratch is a last resort for update failures.
The browser cache has nothing to do with installing operating system updates.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 9: Software Troubleshooting, Objective 3.2 question 5
note: 220-1102 3.2; mapped to 220-1202 3.4 (PC security issues in the old objectives).

stem: Which of the following browser-related symptoms is typically associated with adware or malware infections?
explanation: Adware or malware infections often result in the appearance of random or frequent pop-up advertisements on web browsers. These popups are usually unwanted and may lead to potentially harmful websites or downloads.
whyWrong: Certificate warnings point to a problem with a site certificate, not to adware on the computer.
Redirection is most often a sign of browser hijacking rather than of adware.
Slow internet speed has many network causes and is not a specific sign of adware.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 9: Software Troubleshooting, Objective 3.2 question 6
note: 220-1102 3.2; mapped to 220-1202 3.4 (PC security issues in the old objectives).

stem: What is the MOST LIKELY cause of receiving repeated certificate warnings when accessing secure websites?
explanation: When a security certificate associated with a website expires, the browser generates certificate warnings to inform the user about the potential security risks. It is important to ensure that websites have up-to-date security certificates.
whyWrong: An outdated browser can have certificate problems, but an expired certificate is the more likely cause.
A firewall that blocks secure traffic stops the connection instead of showing certificate warnings.
DNS cache poisoning is an attack that is much less common than a site certificate that has expired.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 9: Software Troubleshooting, Objective 3.2 question 7
note: 220-1102 3.2; mapped to 220-1202 3.4 (PC security issues in the old objectives).

stem: Which browser-related symptom is commonly associated with browser hijacking?
explanation: Browser hijacking is a form of malware attack where the settings of a web browser are modified without the user’s consent, leading to frequent redirection to unwanted websites. This symptom is particularly associated with browser hijacking.
whyWrong: Popups are more typical of adware than of a hijacked browser.
Certificate warnings come from invalid or expired site certificates, not from browser hijacking.
Slow internet speed has many causes and is not a specific sign of browser hijacking.
source: CompTIA A+ Practice Tests Core 1 (220-1101) and Core 2 (220-1102) (Neil) – Chapter 9: Software Troubleshooting, Objective 3.2 question 8
note: 220-1102 3.2; mapped to 220-1202 3.4 (PC security issues in the old objectives).

stem: A user types the bank's web address on her office PC and gets a page that looks almost the same as the bank's site and asks for her login. Other PCs on the same network that use the same DNS servers reach the real site. What is the MOST LIKELY cause?
options: Malicious entries were added to the PC's hosts file
The PC's date and time are set wrong
The browser's pop-up blocker is turned off
The PC's system drive is almost full
explanation: Entries in the hosts file are used before DNS, so they can redirect one computer to a fake site. Because the other PCs use the same DNS servers and work, the problem is on this PC. This kind of pharming aims to steal logins.
whyWrong: A wrong clock causes certificate warnings, not a redirect to a look-alike site.
A disabled pop-up blocker lets new windows open; it does not change where an address goes.
A full drive can make updates fail, but it does not redirect web addresses.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter) – Core 2 Chapter 7: Troubleshooting Operating Systems and Security

stem: A user calls because all of the documents on his laptop now have a strange new extension and will not open. A text file with payment instructions is in every folder, and more files are changing. What should the technician do FIRST?
options: Disconnect the laptop from the network
Pay the ransom to get the decryption key
explanation: These are the signs of ransomware encrypting the files. Disconnecting the laptop first keeps the ransomware from reaching shared drives and other computers. The technician can then remove the malware and restore the files from a backup.
whyWrong: Paying does not guarantee the files come back and does not stop the infection from spreading.
An update does not stop malware that is already running and encrypting files.
Deleting the notes does nothing to stop the encryption or recover the files.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter) – Core 2 Chapter 7: Troubleshooting Operating Systems and Security

stem: While browsing, a user sees a box that looks like a Windows message. It says a serious security error was found and tells her to call a support number right away. The company's antivirus shows no alert. What is the BEST action?
options: Do not call the number, close the message, and run a full antimalware scan
Call the number so support can remove the threat
Turn off the antivirus so the support team can connect
Forward the message to all coworkers as a warning
explanation: A fake desktop alert copies the look of Windows to social engineer the user into calling scammers. The user should not call, and a scan checks for any malware that produced the message. User education helps prevent these scams.
whyWrong: The number reaches scammers who try to sell useless software or get remote access.
Turning off protection helps an attacker and does nothing to fix the problem.
Forwarding spreads panic; the technician should report it through the proper channel.
source: CompTIA A+ Complete Study Guide (Docter) – Core 2 Chapter 7: Troubleshooting Operating Systems and Security
